column4: The clause وَلَا طَعَامٌ إِلَّا مِنْ غِسْلِينٍ repeats the section's strict absence-plus-exception form: the only “food” is itself punishment.
The damned eat from the Zaqqum tree and fill their bellies; bodily filling without nourishment makes explicit the section's distinction between filling a body and relieving its lack.
طَعَامًا ذَا غُصَّةٍ is food that sticks in the throat, another food whose normal life-sustaining function has become torment.
Those who conceal revelation “eat into their bellies nothing but fire”; the eating-and-belly vocabulary turns apparent intake into the very opposite of nourishment.
Those who consume orphans' wealth unjustly are in fact eating fire into their bellies, another exact case of eating that fills the body only with punishment.

The supposed shade is لَا ظَلِيلٍ وَلَا يُغْنِي مِنَ اللَّهَبِ: it neither shades nor avails against flame, exactly the section's image of a thing retaining its name while failing both functions, with the same يُغْنِي construction.
The command to proceed to a three-branched “shade” stages the object whose failure 77:31 then states, just as 88:6 names the food before 88:7 tests its functions.
فَلَيْسَ لَهُ ... حَمِيمٌ begins with absolute deprivation; 69:36 then adds the sole food exception, reproducing the section's ordered movement from “there is none” to “except.”
This ayah says only the sinners eat that ghislin; it completes 69:36 by identifying the punitive food's fitting consumers rather than treating it as ordinary nourishment.
The Zaqqum tree begins another hell-food scene; 44:44 names it food, while its being a tree directly recalls the plant called ضَرِيع.
طَعَامُ الْأَثِيمِ expressly calls Zaqqum “the food of the sinner,” a nourishment-word turned into a designation of punishment.
The food behaves like molten metal boiling in bellies, showing ingestion that injures the body instead of feeding it.
Its boiling is likened to boiling water; this completes the bodily effect of the false food in 44:43-45 and joins punitive food to punitive drink.
The misguided deniers must eat from a tree of Zaqqum, a direct second occurrence of the hell-plant meal.
They fill their bellies from it, repeating the precise boundary developed in the section: fullness can occur without nourishment or relief.
After the Zaqqum they drink boiling water, completing a meal in which both food and drink intensify need and pain.
They drink like desperately thirsty camels; the simile makes the drink's failure to satisfy thirst perceptible, parallel to food that fails hunger.
هَذَا نُزُلُهُمْ calls this damaging meal their “hospitality” on Judgment Day, another normal provision-word made grimly nonfunctional.
The question contrasts true hospitality with the tree of Zaqqum; it explicitly makes quality of provision, rather than the bare availability of something edible, the issue.
Zaqqum is a tree growing in the root of Hell, a hell-grown plant counterpart to the section's dried thorn plant.
Its fruit is made visually repellent before 37:66 describes eating it, marking the plant itself as punishment rather than provision.
A mixture of boiling water follows the belly-filling food of 37:66, completing the food-and-drink torment.
The damned taste neither coolness nor drink; the double negation establishes deprivation before 78:25 supplies its punitive exception.
إِلَّا حَمِيمًا وَغَسَّاقًا answers the absence of drink with boiling water and foul discharge, the same “nothing except a harmful substitute” structure as ضَرِيع.
The person in Hell is made to drink festering water, a liquid provision that deepens suffering rather than relieving thirst.
He gulps but can scarcely swallow it and is approached by death without dying; the ayah spells out the drink's failure even at the act of consumption.
When the damned call for relief, they receive water like molten metal that scorches faces; the offered drink reverses the very relief requested.
حَمِيمٌ وَغَسَّاقٌ are presented for tasting in Hell, another pair of punitive liquids masquerading as provision.

This ayah sets rivers of unspoiled water, milk, wine, and honey against boiling water that cuts the intestines; it contains within one ayah the section's boundary between provision and intake that destroys the body.
Boiling water is poured over the heads of the people of the Fire, beginning a bodily destruction scene that 22:20 carries inward.
The boiling water melts what is in their bellies as well as their skins, reversing the belly-building work the section assigns to food.
They are dragged through boiling water and then burned in the Fire; the liquid belongs to punishment rather than refreshment.
A boiling drink is assigned as recompense, a direct instance of drink serving torment rather than answering bodily need.
The ayah pairs just recompense for believers with a boiling drink for rejecters; the drink is an anti-provision produced by the judgment scene.
The criminals circulate between Hell and boiling water, making the drink inseparable from the fire it ordinarily ought to relieve.

The people of the Fire ask the people of the Garden for water or some of God's provision and are told both are forbidden to rejecters; unrelieved need and true provision confront one another in one scene.
The condemned person did not urge feeding the poor; in the same passage 69:36 gives him only ghislin, making failed human feeding and punitive non-food answer one another.
مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ says his wealth did not avail him; the nearby hell-food scene turns the section's غ ن ي wordplay into a double failure of wealth and food to remove need.
Seven fat cows are eaten by seven lean ones, beside green ears and dry ears; the dream gathers the section's fatness-versus-emaciation and living-versus-dried plant contrasts in one scene.
The dream is repeated as سَبْعِ بَقَرَاتٍ سِمَانٍ consumed by lean cows with green and dry ears, preserving both the س م ن root and the dry-food crisis.
Joseph tells them to leave the harvest in its ears except the little they eat; this gives the dream's fat and dry images their concrete meaning as conserved nourishment.
Seven hard years consume almost all the stored crop, turning the eating imagery of the dream into an extended hunger and depletion scene.
Abraham brings a عِجْلٍ سَمِينٍ, a fat calf offered in hospitality; the س م ن root supplies the abundant, nourishing opposite of food that لَا يُسْمِنُ.
God brings forth pasture, the living plant stage before 87:5 turns it into dark stubble; that transformation closely matches the plant that is called ضَرِيع when dried.
The pasture becomes غُثَاءً أَحْوَىٰ, dried dark debris; it is the closest non-hell plant parallel to the section's emphasis that shibriq acquires its grim name after drying.
Worldly growth pleases its cultivators, then dries, yellows, and becomes debris; the visible passage from lush plant to dry remnant illuminates how ضَرِيع names a plant in its depleted state.
Water produces varied crops that then dry, yellow, and break apart; the ayah stages the precise loss of living plant abundance presupposed by dried ضَرِيع.
Rain-mixed vegetation becomes dry fragments scattered by wind, another direct Quranic rendering of plant matter after nourishment and freshness have gone.

Earth's vegetation flourishes with rain until it is suddenly reaped as though it had not existed; the plant's passage from apparent abundance to nothing supports the section's dried, empty provision image.
After Saba turns away, its two gardens are replaced by bitter fruit, tamarisk, and scant lote; productive vegetation becomes a meager plant provision strikingly close to the dried thorn meal.
“Have you considered what you sow?” opens a crop-provision interrogation whose answer distinguishes true nourishment from a crop that can be made debris.
The question asks whether humans make the crop grow or God does, placing actual food production with the same Provider whom Abraham names in 26:79.
God could make the crop حُطَامًا, shattered dry debris; this is a direct boundary between nourishing vegetation and plant matter like the section's dried thorn.
The cultivators would be left lamenting their loss, giving the ruined crop's human consequence rather than leaving the dry-plant image abstract.
بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ names the result as deprivation, the state a food that does not remove hunger leaves intact.
The interrogation turns from sown food to the water people drink, matching the section's secondary drink sense of ضَرِيع.
The ayah asks whether people send drinking water down or God does, identifying the source of the relief absent from hell's punitive drink.
God could make the water bitter; this explicit reversal shows that a substance can keep the appearance of drink while losing its relieving function.
أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ states the exact successful opposite: God feeds them out of hunger, so true food performs the removal that ضَرِيع cannot.
Adam is promised أَلَّا تَجُوعَ in the Garden; absence of hunger defines complete provision against the hell meal that leaves hunger untouched.
The Garden also removes thirst and exposure to heat, completing 20:118's picture of bodily needs answered rather than aggravated.
Abraham names God as the one who feeds and gives drink; the paired verbs identify true provision against the section's non-food and its secondary “thin drink” sense.
A secure town receives abundant provision, then is made to taste hunger and fear after ingratitude; it reverses 106:4 and makes hunger the felt withdrawal of real food.
Saba is told to eat from its Lord's provision amid two gardens and a good land; 34:16 then reverses this abundant food landscape into bitter, sparse growth.
كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا هَنِيئًا is the paired answer to 69:36: the righteous are told to eat and drink pleasantly where the condemned receive ghislin.
The recipient is “in a pleasing life” before being told to eat and drink in 69:24; that good condition realizes the section's dictionary observation that a well-fed person is in a good state.
The God-fearing are in real shade and springs, directly reversing the non-shading “shade” of 77:30-31.
They receive fruits they desire; the continuing contrast replaces the condemned person's false shelter and provision with wanted food.
“Eat and drink pleasantly” supplies the functional meal opposite the earlier shade that does not avail against flame.
Gardens and grapes begin the reward scene paired with 78:24-25's absence of coolness and punitive drink.
A brimming cup supplies the drink-side reversal of the boiling water and ghassaq in 78:25.
The secure inhabitants of the Garden call for every fruit, the same surah's direct abundance-and-safety opposite to Zaqqum as the sinner's food.
Chosen fruit in the reward scene stands opposite the same surah's compelled eating from Zaqqum.
Desired bird meat adds nourishing choice to the paired reward meal, against bellies forcibly filled from the hell tree in 56:53.
Fruits and honor define the provision to which 37:62 compares Zaqqum when it asks which is the better hospitality.
Abundant fruit and drink in the Garden form the same surah's direct counter-scene to the boiling water and ghassaq of 38:57.
Fruit and desired meat are supplied to the blessed, showing food as wanted provision rather than compulsory torment.
الجُوع is a divinely announced trial alongside fear and loss; unlike the final fixed hunger of the section, this hunger is limited by “something of” and calls for patient response.
After the hard years comes rain and pressing of produce; the ayah completes the fat/lean, green/dry sequence with restored liquid and abundance.
وَهُوَ يُطْعِمُ وَلَا يُطْعَمُ distinguishes the God who feeds from creatures who need feeding, clarifying the section's opposition between need and true sufficiency.
God wants neither provision from creatures nor that they feed Him; this is absolute needlessness beside the section's hungry bodies and deficient food.
Naming God الرَّزَّاق completes 51:57: the One who needs no food is Himself the steadfast Provider.
Water from heaven becomes drink and vegetation for grazing, combining true drink with living pasture against thin punitive drink and a dried thorn.
The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits, a many-sided plant provision opposite the single dry plant imposed in Hell.
Pure, palatable milk comes from livestock; it realizes the abundance heard in the section's secondary sense of ضَرِيع as a large-uddered ewe and counters its thin-drink sense.
Livestock give drink from their bellies, many benefits, and meat to eat; milk, food, and bodily benefit unite where ضَرِيع supplies none.
Subdued livestock are ridden and eaten, making the herd an actual source of nourishment rather than merely the unused abundance suggested by “large-uddered ewe.”
Livestock provide benefits and drinks, completing 36:72's food scene and directly activating the udder-and-drink secondary meanings developed in the section.
Rain brings forth diverse pairs of plants, the living and varied plant-world opposite to one dried, foul food plant.
“Eat and pasture your livestock” identifies those plants as effective nourishment for people and herds.
Rain-raised gardens contain abundant fruits from which people eat, directly opposing a plant that neither fattens nor removes hunger.
The Sinai tree produces oil and relish for eaters; this is a plant defined by bodily benefit and palatability, the precise functional opposite of ضَرِيع.
Water driven to barren land produces crops eaten by livestock and people; the ayah explicitly carries dry ground through growth to nourishment.
Dead earth is revived and yields grain from which people eat, making plant life perform precisely the feeding function missing from ضَرِيع.
Gardens of palms and grapes and flowing springs expand the grain scene into abundant food and drink.
People eat the gardens' fruit though their hands did not create it, pointing from effective food back to its Provider.
Blessed water descends and grows gardens and harvest grain, the life-giving beginning of a provision scene opposite the dried thorn.
Lofty palms with layered clusters add visibly full fruit to the provision scene.
رِزْقًا لِّلْعِبَادِ names the growth as provision and joins it to reviving dead land, the reverse of plant matter emptied of nourishment.
Abundant pouring water begins the growth sequence, contrasting both the dry plant and the hell drinks that cannot relieve.
The water brings forth grain and plants, productive vegetation rather than dried thorn.
Dense gardens complete the rain-to-food scene with abundance.
The earth's water and pasture are brought forth together, pairing drink with food for grazing animals.
مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ names water and pasture as provision for people and livestock, directly answering the section's plant, hunger, and ewe imagery.
The command to look at one's food opens a detailed account of how real nourishment is made, a deliberate counter-image to food that fails as food.
Water is poured abundantly as the first cause in the food sequence, joining nourishment and drink.
The earth is split open so food can emerge, advancing the production scene toward edible plants.
Grain is grown from it, the staple nourishment opposite a dried thorn.
Grapes and fresh herbage extend the food scene to human produce and grazing vegetation.
Olives and palms add oil-bearing and fruit-bearing trees to the abundance.
Dense gardens supply the cultivated setting for the foods enumerated around this ayah.
Fruit and pasture place human food beside livestock feed, especially pertinent to the section's large-uddered-ewe echo.
The whole sequence is provision for people and their livestock, explicitly naming the beneficiaries of the effective food system.
Rain produces green growth, grain, date clusters, vines, olives, and pomegranates; this ripening abundance is the plant-world reverse of dried ضَرِيع.
God sends water and brings forth fruits as provision, directly joining the Provider to food that genuinely answers need.
Rain and fruits are made رِزْقًا لَّكُمْ, a concise creation-to-provision chain opposite a plant offered without nourishment.
إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ makes feeding on a day of severe hunger the saving ascent, the ethical reverse of leaving someone with food that cannot remove hunger.
The righteous give food they value to the poor, orphan, and captive; food here truly passes toward need rather than preserving deprivation.
Rejecters answer a command to spend from God's provision by asking whether they should feed one God could feed; the ayah exposes misuse of divine provision language to leave hunger unanswered.
People are الفُقَرَاءُ to God while God is الغَنِيُّ; this directly states the need-versus-sufficiency opposition used by the section to explain both ضراعة and يُغْنِي.
اللَّهُ الْغَنِيُّ وَأَنتُمُ الْفُقَرَاءُ repeats the same absolute contrast between divine sufficiency and creaturely need that the failed food cannot cure.
God found the addressee عَائِلًا and made him sufficient, using أَغْنَى for an actual passage from need to sufficiency rather than the failure expressed by لَا يُغْنِي.
وَأَنَّهُ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ attributes enrichment and sufficiency to God, the positive source of the state the hell food cannot produce.
The miser “deems himself self-sufficient” with اسْتَغْنَىٰ; 92:11 will expose that imagined sufficiency when his wealth cannot avail him.
وَمَا يُغْنِي عَنْهُ مَالُهُ says wealth does not avail when he falls, joining the section's functional يُغْنِي sense to the dictionary sense of wealth and showing both fail together.
مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ repeats the pointed paradox that wealth itself does not make its owner free of ultimate need.

The orphan-guardian rule places غَنِيًّا opposite فَقِيرًا and allows the poor guardian to “eat” reasonably; it concretely joins economic sufficiency, need, and eating, the three senses unfolded in the section.
The section's dictionary branch defines ضراعة as displayed extreme need; يَتَضَرَّعُونَ here is the hoped-for pleading after hardship and adversity make that need felt.
تَضَرَّعُوا names the humble pleading that should have followed punishment, while hard hearts prevent acknowledgment of need; it continues the ضراعة branch developed in the section.
Peoples are seized with hardship and adversity so that they might humble themselves; the ض ر ع form turns affliction into manifest need, the human-state sense heard beside ضَرِيع.
Even punishment does not make them submit or يَتَضَرَّعُونَ; the refusal to display need is a significant reversal of the section's dictionary sense of ضراعة.
Wealth and children لَن تُغْنِيَ عَنْهُمْ against God; possessions fail to create the needlessness that the section's غ ن ي definition associates with possessions.
The same warning is repeated: wealth and children will not avail against God, fixing a boundary on material “sufficiency.”
Neither wealth nor children will avail against God; this is another concrete case where what appears to supply worldly sufficiency fails in the judgment setting.

The unknowing count restrained poor people أَغْنِيَاءَ; the ayah distinguishes apparent sufficiency from real hidden need, sharpening the section's concern with what food is called and what condition it actually leaves.
If believers fear poverty, God promises to enrich them from His bounty; this uses the غ ن ي family for relief of material need, the successful sense denied in لَا يُغْنِي مِن جُوعٍ.
If those marrying are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty; the promise supplies a social instance of need genuinely removed.
أَن رَّآهُ اسْتَغْنَىٰ identifies perceived self-sufficiency as the ground of human transgression, a moral boundary around the section's dictionary sense of being without need.
Jesus and Mary both “used to eat food”; the ordinary need to eat marks creaturely dependence and helps explain why food that does not answer hunger is such complete deprivation.
“Who could provide for you if He withheld His provision?” makes food-sufficiency contingent on the Provider, the premise stated personally by Abraham in 26:79.

Many creatures cannot carry their own provision, yet God provides for them and for people; the animal-provision scene resonates with the section's plant and sheep senses without depending on a shared food word.
“We did not feed the poor” is given as a reason for entering Saqar, a second concrete link between refusal of nourishing food and the eater's later punishment.
Failure to urge feeding the poor names a social withholding of food; it is the worldly human counterpart to the section's final scene of need left unrelieved.
The one who denies judgment does not urge feeding the poor, tying disbelief to allowing another's food-need to remain exactly what it was.
